extracted.intended_audience: readers of Rabelais / literary scholars / translators
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted chapters from Rabelais' Pantagruel (translation) discussing judicial pardon, the use of chance in judgment, signs of prophetic inspiration, and oracle-interpretation; a satirical literary narrative rather than a formal guideline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for pardoning Bridlegoose
rubrics_metrics.description: Pantagruel beseecheth that Bridlegoose 'should be pardoned' and sets two conditions: 'First, that he satisfy, or put a sufficient surety for the satisfaction of the party wronged by the injustice of the sentence in question.' 'Secondly, that for his subsidiary aid in the weighty charge of administrating justice you would be pleased to appoint and assign unto him some pretty little virtuous counsellor, younger, learneder, and wiser than he, by the square and rule of whose advice he may regulate, guide, temper, and moderate in times coming all his judiciary procedures.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pantagruel frames these as practical and equitable remedies: compensate the injured party (or provide surety) and supply an advisor to temper future sentences; alternatively Pantagruel offers to employ Bridlegoose if the court chooses to depose him. The surrounding argument appeals to Bridlegoose's old age, simplicity, and long prior record of fair judgments ('these forty years and upwards ... so evenly balanced in the scales of uprightness').

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal excuses accepted by statute and common laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Pantagruel: 'In the first place, his old age; secondly, his simplicity; to both which qualities our statute and common laws, civil and municipal together, allow many excuses for any slips or escapes which, through the invincible imperfection of either, have been inconsiderately stumbled upon by a person so qualified.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text presents age and simplicity as recognized mitigating factors in law, justifying leniency for lapses that arise from those conditions. This is used rhetorically to argue for pardon and to contextualize judicial error as sometimes excusable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satisfactory record as mitigation (single error outweighed by long service)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pantagruel argues that 'this one, sole, and single fault of his ought to be quite forgotten, abolished, and swallowed up by that immense and vast ocean of just dooms and sentences which heretofore he hath given and pronounced; his demeanours, for these forty years and upwards that he hath been a judge, having been so evenly balanced in the scales of uprightness...'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A long history of equitable judgments and public confirmation of past decisions is offered as a substantive ground to excuse a single mistake; the metaphor of a drop in a river emphasizes proportionality in evaluating a judge's overall record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptability of referring hard cases to chance (dice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bridlegoose 'had plainly confessed his final judging and determinating of suits of law by the mere chance and fortune of the dice.' Pantagruel conjectures this is defensible where judges face 'antinomies, contrarieties, ... contradictions' of law and where 'by the providence aforesaid the best chance might fall to him whose action was uprightest.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text presents throwing dice as an epistemic/ethical recourse when human deliberation cannot resolve balanced, knotty disputes: submitting to 'the divine decree' via aleatory lot may be preferable to a corrupt or arbitrary human decision. Talmudic and providential arguments are invoked to justify aleatory methods in certain judicial perplexities.

rubrics_metrics.name: When chance is preferable to corrupt courts
rubrics_metrics.description: Pantagruel: 'it were better ... that parties at variance in any juridical case should in the dark march upon caltrops than submit the determination of what is their right to such unhallowed sentences and horrible decrees' — referring to a parliament 'whose principal direction in all law matters comes to their hands from one Tribonian ... [who] sell laws ... as at an outroop or putsale.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage functions as a critique of legal corruption: when courts are venal or manipulated (laws sold, fragmentarily applied), resorting to chance or other nonstandard methods may be less objectionable than accepting corrupt adjudication. This is an anti-pattern warning about corrupted legal institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs and gestures indicating prophetic/vaticinal inspiration
rubrics_metrics.description: The text lists bodily signs that 'should by us all be judged to proceed from, and be quickened and suscitated by, the coming and inspiration of the prophetizing and fatidical spirit': 'a little frenzy and a head-shaking ... shakings and tremblings ... wagging his head ... shrugging of the shoulders, and jectigation of the whole body.' It cites the Pythian divineress shaking laurel, Heliogabalus making an idol's head shake, Plautus's examples, Catullus's Menades, and the Galli.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple classical and medical authorities are marshalled to treat head-shaking, body agitation, and convulsive gestures as marks of prophetic ecstasy; the author also records alternative (physiological) explanations (trembling from burden or weakness) and mnemonic uses (teachers shaking pupils) — thus the text presents both cultural/sign-based criteria and sceptical/medical counterpoints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of head-wagging undermines prophetic claim
rubrics_metrics.description: The learned lawyer Julian, when asked whether a slave might be esteemed sound if he had prophesied 'yet without a noddle-shaking concussion,' answered that 'seeing there was no head-wagging at the time of his predictions, he might be held for sound and compotent enough.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This positions head-shaking as a necessary (in some authorities' views) concomitant of genuine prophetic inspiration; lacking the physical sign is taken as evidence against ecstatic inspiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting oracles and foolish utterances by gesture and context
rubrics_metrics.description: Triboulet's gestures and cryptic words ('By God, God, mad fool, beware the monk, Buzansay hornpipe!') are read by Pantagruel and Panurge as prognostications: warnings of cuckoldry, a wife given to drink, or other future domestic states. Panurge treats the returned bottle as a sign too ('He put the bottle in my hand and restored it me again' — interpreted as wife's drinking or as empty to mean something else).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage illustrates a hermeneutic for oracles: combine the spoken fragment, physical gestures (thwack, flirt on the nose, head wagging), and contextual tokens (an empty bottle, a returned gift) to derive a practical prediction. It also shows conflicting interpretations (Pantagruel vs Panurge), highlighting ambiguity and the social practice of allegorical reading of fools' speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical preparations / companions for seeking an oracle
rubrics_metrics.description: Pantagruel lists preparations before setting out: 'First, let us send back Triboulet to Blois. Secondly, our design must be backed with the advice and counsel of the king my father. And, lastly, it is most needful and expedient for us that we search for and find out some sibyl to serve us for a guide, truchman, and interpreter.' Panurge suggests Xenomanes and a Lanternesse as suitable companions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a narrative 'checklist' for a voyage to consult an oracle, the priorities are: remove unhelpful fools, obtain sovereign approval/advice, and secure an interpreter/sibyl; also recruit local guides and useful companions (Xenomanes, Lanternesse). The text frames these as prudent preparations for a perilous, advice-seeking journey.
